groups.title: Questions 17–20
groups.instruction: Choose the correct answers from the box, from A–G, next to questions

transcript.text: Next week is our town's International Week, which has been going on annually for several
years.
Today we have George Johnson, the organizer of International Week, to talk about it.
George, how did it all begin?
Well, I was with a group of businessmen in town one February day, five years ago, and we
were discussing what we could do for livening things up in August when the weather is good,
and the kids are out of school till September.
And someone said, hey, we've got people from all over the world living here, let's have
an international celebration and get people to show off things about their home country.
And we all agreed.
The first year, the celebration lasted just one day, and it featured three countries.
It was a great success and was written about in our local newspaper.
And so the next year, even though it costs more, the organizers expanded it to an international
week, and so many people were eager to feature their countries.
On each of the first six days of the week, one country is designated to star.
And then on the seventh day, weather permitting, we have a street party near the town hall
with music provided by the radio station and food and games.
Everyone has a ball.
Of course, we move it to the school gym if it rains like last year, but nobody minds.
Our year starts in January, when we ask for applications.
To apply to have a day for their country, people don't need to belong to a particular
country association.
They can just be a group who identified themselves with a particular country.
They submit a formal plan to us.
They don't need to worry at this stage about funding, but some grants are available.
The organizing committee has to select the ones with the best ideas.
The organizing committee arranges for places for the country to do whatever they want.
Unfortunately, for large outdoor activities, we aren't allowed to use the local stadium
because they've got other commitments.
But the community center lets us use its parking lot.
The hall is kind of small, but it has been kind enough to permit us to make use of its
classrooms.
Local people have been very generous.
A lot of business people let us have things like tables and amplifiers for the week.
The organizing committee handles all the administration, and the town library has
been great about featuring books about the countries.
Before you hear the rest of the program, you have some time to look at questions 17-20.
Now, for each country's day, we ask them to have one special event like a show or exhibition
or demonstration.
For example, some people could show how they make traditional handicrafts.
Or it might just be an exhibition, say photographs of the country.
Interesting.
Now, what are the special events this year?
Fantastic things.
Monday is Mexico Day, and these ladies and gentlemen are going to put on a show that's
hotter than those chili peppers they're famous for eating.
They'll be singing and playing songs, and those drums will make you want to get up and
move around.
Then Tuesday is South Africa Day, and they've got an exhibition of dresses and robes used
in traditional ceremonies and dances, and they are magnificent.
Apparently, some of them are worth more than their weight in gold.
Next, Wednesday is Indonesia Day.
They have an exhibition where you'll definitely get your money's worth.
Two ladies will put on their chef's hat to demonstrate how they prepare those dishes
and sauces they're famous for.
Let's see.
That brings us to Thursday, Canada Day.
We think of them as fit outdoorsmen and ice hockey players, but they've arranged to
have some of their countrymen show us how they use just a knife and blocks of wood from
native American trees to make absolutely lovely statues of birds and bears and other
animals famous in local legends.
So next is Friday, Italy Day.
That is the end of section two.
You now have half a minute to check your answers.
